essentialQuestion.source: How can a computer learn from examples, and why do the examples matter?

learningGoal.source: Explain how a model learns from labelled examples, and why relevant, correctly labelled examples and a test on new examples matter.

warmUp.question.source: You want to teach a young child to tell a healthy leaf from a sick leaf. What would you do?

evidence.label.source: Fictional example created for this lesson.

evidence.question.source: What changed when the model had more examples, and what did the fresh test show?

evidence.cards.0.rows.0.1.source: 2 examples: a big dark green leaf (healthy) and a brown leaf with spots (sick)

evidence.cards.0.rows.1.1.source: 6 examples: the 2 from Round 1, plus 2 more healthy and 2 more sick leaves that look different

evidence.cards.0.rows.2.1.source: 8 examples, including 2 long, striped leaves from a new plant

activity.instructions.source: Teach the model by giving each example leaf a label: healthy or sick. Then test it on new leaves, round by round, and see how many it gets right. Nothing you do here is sent anywhere.

activity.examples.7.description.source: Long thin brown leaf with spots

activity.tests.6.description.source: Long thin leaf with pale stripes

activity.tests.7.description.source: Long thin leaf with pale stripes

activity.rounds.0.debrief.source: The model got 4 of 6 right. It had only two leaves to compare with, so it mixed up the small new leaf and the yellow leaf.

activity.rounds.1.debrief.source: Now the model got all 6 right. The new examples showed it leaves that looked different.

activity.rounds.2.debrief.source: Both striped leaves are healthy, but the model said “sick”. None of its examples looked like them.

activity.rounds.3.debrief.source: With examples of the new plant, the model got all 8 right. But the team had already seen these test leaves, and the test is small. To check fairly, test it on leaves nobody has used yet.

activity.rounds.4.debrief.source: On four leaves nobody had used, the model got 3 of 4 right. It called a long, thin leaf that was turning yellow “healthy”, because it looked most like the striped healthy example. A fresh test shows what a model still gets wrong, and four leaves are still a small test.

activity.freePlay.source: After Round 4, the learner can take examples out, or change a label, and test again. The model follows the learner's labels, even when they differ from the gardener's.

activity.explainGuess.source: After each guess, show the example the model thought was most like the new leaf: “It looked most like this example, so the model said sick.”

read.sections.0.heading.source: A model learns from labelled examples

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI learns a bit like studying with flashcards. At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data: pictures of leaves, each with the correct answer, called a label, either “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses these examples to build a model. It uses the model to predict the label of a leaf it has never seen. This is machine learning. Nobody writes the rule “spots mean sick”; the computer finds patterns like that in the examples. Learning from labelled examples is called supervised learning, one kind of machine learning. It is an old idea. A machine called the perceptron learned from marked cards in 1958, and researchers studied this lesson's method in 1967. It became far more useful after 2010, with more data and faster computers.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: At Sunrise Garden, people collected training data. Each leaf picture has the right answer, called a label: “healthy” or “sick”. The computer uses them to make a model. It uses the model to guess. This is machine learning. Nobody tells it “spots mean sick”. It finds that in the examples. Learning from labels is called supervised learning. It is an old idea. A machine did it in 1958. This method was studied in 1967. It grew more useful after 2010.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Better examples, then a fair test

read.sections.1.text.source: The first model learned from only two examples. It guesses in a simple way: it finds the example most like the new leaf and copies its label. On six new leaves it got four right. It called a small, light green leaf “sick”, because it had too few examples to compare with. Then the team added four leaves that looked different, and it got all six right. But the team had already looked at those six test leaves while they improved the model. A fair test uses leaves that nobody has used yet. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three of them right. It called a long leaf that was turning yellow “healthy”. A fresh test shows what a model still gets wrong. Four leaves are still a small test.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The first model had only two examples. It finds the example most like a new leaf. It copies that label. It got four of six new leaves right. It had too few examples. Then the team added four different leaves. Now it got all six right. But the team had already seen those six leaves. A fair test uses new leaves. The team kept four leaves aside. The model got three of them right. A new test shows what it still gets wrong.

read.sections.2.text.source: Real tools work in a similar way, at a much bigger size. In Tanzania, researchers from the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Penn State University made a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from pictures of the leaves of cassava, a food crop, taken in Tanzanian fields, and it works without the internet. When researchers tested it on plants in the field, it did much better when it looked at six leaves from a plant than at one. Relevant examples with correct labels help a model. More examples alone do not always help: a wrong label can make guesses worse. And a tool like this only helps people check leaves. Farmers and experts still decide what to do.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Real tools work like this too, but they are much bigger. In Tanzania, researchers made a free phone app called Nuru. It learned from pictures of cassava leaves. Cassava is a plant that people grow for food. It works without the internet. In tests, it did better when it looked at six leaves from a plant. Good examples with the right labels help. A wrong label can make it worse. The app helps people check leaves. People still decide what to do.

write.prompt.source: Explain why the Sunrise Garden team kept four leaves aside for a fresh test. Use one number from the lesson.

write.sentenceStarters.2.source: On the fresh test, the model ...

write.example.source: The team had already seen the first six test leaves while they improved the model, so getting all six right did not prove much. A fair test uses leaves that nobody has used yet. On the four fresh leaves, the model got three right and called a leaf that was turning yellow “healthy”. The fresh test showed a mistake the team would not have noticed. Four leaves are still a small test, so they should test it on more.

speak.partnerTask.source: Tell your partner how you would train a model to sort two kinds of things, like ripe and unripe fruit. Your partner asks, “How will you test it fairly?” Then switch.

speak.independentTask.source: Say out loud three steps: collect labelled examples, train the model, test it on new examples. Give one example for each step.

watch.why.source: It shows a computer learning to tell shapes apart from labelled examples, the same idea as the leaf model.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: How could a computer learn to tell two shapes apart?

watch.afterQuestion.source: Why is it hard to write exact rules for a shape, like the letter X?

watch.summary.source: This video explains computer vision. Computer vision is how a computer finds meaning in pictures. A computer does not see a picture like you do. It sees a number for each tiny dot of colour. Writing exact rules for a shape, like the letter X, does not work well, because people draw an X in many ways. With machine learning, the computer learns from many labelled examples instead. It is like learning with flashcards. The computer guesses, checks the answer and slowly gets better. Harder pictures, like faces, need bigger models. The video shows farm robots that tell crops from weeds. It also warns about a problem. If the training data leaves some people out, the tool can fail for them. So training data must be large and varied.

watch.keyPoints.0.source: A computer sees a picture as numbers, one for each tiny dot.

watch.keyPoints.1.source: With machine learning, a computer learns from many labelled examples, like flashcards.

watch.keyPoints.2.source: If the training data leaves some people out, the tool can fail for them.

watch.contentNote.source: About six minutes, longer than most Thinkerwell videos. The speakers work for a farm-robot company and a car company and name them. Near the end, it says face recognition can fail for groups of people left out of the training data; Lessons 8 and 12 come back to this. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

educatorNotes.0.source: The leaf model is now an optional extension (Justin's brief of 4 November 2026): the reading teaches learning from examples and the fair test, and the activity is folded under “Try it yourself” for learners who want more. It has all four rounds and free play. On paper: one learner is the model and may only copy the label of the most similar example card; keep the four Round 4 cards face down until the fair test.

educatorNotes.1.source: The model is deliberately simple: a nearest-neighbour model (k = 1) that copies the label of the most similar example. It is one supervised method; Cover and Hart's 1967 paper studied this rule, and Rosenblatt's perceptron, shown in July 1958, also learned from labelled examples. Real AI is far bigger, and other kinds of machine learning don't need a label on every example, but the points about examples and testing are the same.

educatorNotes.2.source: Nuru: the evaluation in Tanzania (Mrisho and others, a bioRxiv preprint from 2020) found the app more accurate with six leaves per plant than with one leaf image. The lesson gives no percentages on purpose: the study's numbers depend on which test and which disease. The app supports diagnosis; it does not replace extension workers or farmers' decisions.

educatorNotes.3.source: If a learner labels an example differently from the gardener in the extension, the model follows the learner. That is a good moment to ask: who decides the right label?
